items.title: ‘Focker-In-Law’ review: Even Ariana Grande’s comedy chops can’t save this legacy sequel
items.summary:
I t’s 26 years since Ben Stiller was strapped into the lie detector test for Meet The Parents , the 2000 hit that helped establish co-star Robert De Niro as a comedic force after years of prestige drama. Two sequels followed, Meet The Fockers and Little Fockers , which were both financially successful but critically mauled ( Little Fockers achieved a horrific 10 per cent rating on Rotten Tomatoes ). Sixteen years on from the last movie, Ben Stiller is getting the band back together, but can this family reunion run smoother than the last one?

READ MORE: Ariana Grande – ‘Petal’ review: conflicted pop songs under the spotlight 

We rejoin Greg Focker (Stiller) as a doting father of two grown children, preparing to travel to see his father-in-law Jack (De Niro) for his birthday party. Greg is especially anxious as his son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) is bringing his new girlfriend, Olivia ( Ariana Grande ) to meet the family. Olivia is a life coach and former FBI hostage negotiator who immediately charms everyone, except for Greg. Suspicious of her motives and jealous of her instant rapport with Jack, he sets out to scupper Henry’s planned proposal.

Directed by regular John Hamburg who wrote the first three movies, this legacy sequel plays out exactly like the old films. Broadly following the same plot as the first movie, Stiller runs an assault course of slapstick gags designed to make him look as ridiculous as possible, while the rest of the cast mostly react to his hijinks. There was an opportunity to have Greg come full circle, becoming the stern future in-law to Grande’s…
items.t: ‘Focker-In-Law’ review: Even Ariana Grande’s comedy chops can’t save this legacy sequel

items.summary:

Past SCL Lifetime Achievement Award honorees include Stephen Schwartz, Charles Fox, Giorgio Moroder, Quincy Jones, Danny Elfman, Bill Conti, Lalo Schifrin, Philip Glass, Alan Menken and Ginny Mancini.

Newman’s many honors include seven Grammys, three Primetime Emmys and two Academy Awards. He was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2002 and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2013.

Hamlisch won three Oscars, four Grammys, four Primetime Emmys, a Tony and two Golden Globes. He shared the Pulitzer Prize for Drama for the 1975 Broadway smash A Chorus Line. He died in 2012 at age 68.

Hagen composed the theme songs for dozens of TV shows, including The Andy Griffith Show, The Dick Van Dyke Show and That Girl. Hagen won a Primetime Emmy in 1968 for his work on I Spy . He was inducted into the Television Academy Hall of Fame in 2011, and died in 2008 at age 88.

items.summary:

items.title: FKA Twigs and Patti Smith added to Gasometer grand opening as we go inside the “new cultural landmark for Northern Europe”
items.summary:
FKA Twigs , Marina Abramović and Patti Smith are among the new names added to the grand opening of Stockholm’s ambitious new Gasometer venue, as NME takes an early look inside what’s being called the “new cultural landmark for Northern Europe”.

As announced last month, the new live music space in the Swedish capital will open its doors on Wednesday March 17, 2027 . An historic former gas holder designed by prominent architect Ferdinand Boberg built in 1899, the impressive and towering structure is being renovated into a multi-purpose, multi-venue entertainment space as a central part of a much wider urban regeneration scheme. With around €100million (£83.6million) investment, the transformed venue is promising to bring together architecture, live entertainment and state-of-the-art audio and visual technology.

Gasometer will be made up of two main gig spaces: the pillar-free main theatre auditorium with a capacity of 1,700-2,300, and ‘The Dome’ above it which will offer 1,000 fans a unique venue for live performances, fine dining and immersive events.

Gasometer design plans. CREDIT: Press 
 It was previously confirmed that composer Jacob Mühlrad and visual artist and creative director Alexander Wessely will be the first to host events there when the venue opens its doors for events between March 17 and March 20. Now, it’s been announced that both FKA twigs and Patti Smith will be performing their own music with new orchestral arrangements by Mühlrad in in ALEPH – a four-act experience that brings together classical and contemporary music, performance, movement and visual…

items.title: AC/DC, Blondie and Kylie Minogue lead tributes after beloved music promoter Molly Meldrum dies, aged 83
items.summary:
AC/DC , Blondie and Kylie Minogue are among a host of stars who have paid tribute to music promoter Molly Meldrum who has died, aged 83.

The Australian broadcaster and record producer died at Epworth Hospital in Richmond after a long illness, according to Billboard . “He was deeply loved by his long-term partner, Yan Wongngam, his family and all who knew him,” his family said in a statement.

They described Meldrum as the “heartbeat, the champion and the spirit of Australian music”, saying he had influenced generations of musicians and music fans.

“Affectionately dubbed ‘the Guru’, he shaped not only the sound of a nation but also the dreams of generations who grew up with his voice guiding them,” they added.

A cause of death has yet to be revealed.

AC/DC were among those who paid tribute to Meldrum. “Remembering Ian “Molly” Meldrum Championing AC/DC since 1974,” the band wrote on their Instagram.

As host of Australia’s Countdown music programme, Meldrum championed local and international artists from Minogue, ​INXS to ABBA from 1974 for 13 years.

View this post on Instagram 

Minogue recalled her time on the show adding: “I was over the moon to be in the Countdown audience one time and by my late teens I was on the show! (and Molly visited us in ‘Neighbours’!) The stories are many and there was never a dull moment!

“He championed so many Aussie artists and welcomed international artists to Australia in his own wonderful and inimitable way. I’m so grateful for his unwavering love and support. Vale Molly. I’m going to turn the music up in your honour.”

View this…
items.t: AC/DC, Blondie and Kylie Minogue lead tributes after beloved music promoter Molly Meldrum dies, aged 83

“I’m very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to unfortunate incident last night Manchester [sic]” he wrote on his Instagram Stories Monday.

“I just wanna make sure everyone is safe and the next show goes on properly. My heart and prayers are with with [sic] everyone that was injured last night @ co-op live. The only thing I love more than creating music is performing for my fans ! STOP BRINGING BULLS–T INTO MY SHOWS!! it ain’t cool see you soon London. Love you guys. DT.”

The Houston-born rapper was performing at Manchester’s Co-op Live on Sunday (Nov. 22) when roughly 40 minutes into the set, the incident took place. Greater Manchester Police believe the substance to be tear gas, per the BBC .

More 12,000 people were evacuated from the venue and a major incident was declared. The North West Ambulance service said 80 people were treated for “eye and respiratory symptoms,” with one person admitted to hospital.

items.title: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ review: a hollow retread of the cult dystopian classic
items.summary:
B ack in 1982, Blade Runner predicted that we’d all now be living in a dystopian nightmare world without the ability to tell what was real and what was AI …

READ MORE: The best TV shows of 2026… so far! 

Ridley Scott ’s adaptation of Philip K Dick’s cyberpunk noir novel became an all-time cult classic – shaping sci-fi design enough to get Elon Musk sued for copying it . Denis Villeneuve ’s 2017 sequel somehow managed to match it. Sadly, Amazon’s stylish but lifeless new TV series doesn’t add anything worthwhile to the franchise and feels worryingly like a win for the machines instead of the humans.

Showrunner Silka Luisa flips the original premise to better fit our new OpenAI future. The robot “replicants” won the war and we’re the new underclass, with those not surrendering now hunted by cyborg cops. It’s a neat twist, but it’s one that makes the show feel a whole lot less unique as it falls into the trope of a dozen other sci-fi stories.

Hunter Schafer gets her first post- Euphoria lead as Cora, a human on the run who hides her identity by posing as a replicant detective – finding herself partnered up in the LAPD with Michelle Yeoh ’s almost aged-out robot Olwen. A larger backstory unfolds across eight hours, with Cora and Olwen getting tangled up in a MacGuffin involving lost memories, corrupt leaders and a quasi-philosophical quest to preserve artificial life, all played out here as a moody cop show with flying cars.

Twice as long as everything we’ve seen of the franchise so far, the series oddly doesn’t make the world seem any bigger. Strikingly designed and…
items.t: ‘Blade Runner 2099’ review: a hollow retread of the cult dystopian classic

items.title: Live music to be banned from rooftop of The Beatles’ Saville Row London fan experience
items.summary:
Live music is set to banned from the rooftop where The Beatles played their final public performance in 1969.

READ MORE: The Beatles: every song ranked in order of greatness 

The Fab Four famously played on what was Apple Corps’ headquarters on 3 Savile Row in London on the site of the studio where ‘ Let It Be ‘ was recorded.

Earlier this year, the company founded by the band, announced it was converting the building into a seven-floor “cultural experience and exhibition” celebrating The Beatles, with a basement café-bar on the site of the studio where they recorded their last album.

Launching in 2027, it will allow fans access to seven floors of never-before-seen material from Apple Corps’ extensive archives, rotating exhibitions, a fan store, as well as a recreation of the original studio where ‘Let it Be’ was recorded.

The Beatles’ famous rooftop concert at Apple HQ in 1969. CREDIT: PRESS 
 Apple Corps is forecasting up to 900 visitors each weekday and 1,140 on weekends, entering in timed slots of 20 people every 10 minutes.

But according to draft conditions, no live music can be played on the terrace and any amplified music or speech should be noise limited, BBC News reports. A two-metre-high acoustic barrier has also been proposed

The Savile Row Bespoke Association, which represents the street’s bespoke tailors, has objected to the plans stating they are in conflict with the Savile Row Special Policy Area planning designation that aims to protect bespoke tailoring on the street, according to BBC News .

It has also warned that narrow pavements “would lead to…

items.title: Portishead join ‘No Music For Genocide’ campaign as music disappears from platforms in Israel
items.summary:
Portishead have joined the ‘No Music For Genocide’ campaign and pulled their music from streaming platforms in Israel.

The trip-hop band’s three albums are no longer available on Spotify , Apple Music and the band’s YouTube page in the country in recent days, according to a recent report by Israeli newsletter Haaretz .

‘No Music For Genocide’ have since confirmed that this is the case and the band have joined their campaign on their Instagram Story.

Portishead’s Geoff Barrow also took to his own Instagram Story to share a post by Annie Lennox showing Gaza in 2023 and 2026. “And people wonder why we boycott Israel,” Barrow captioned the post.

The ‘No Music For Genocide’ campaign is a cultural boycott initiative encouraging artists and rights-holders to pull their music from streaming platforms in Israel in response to the UN declared genocide in Gaza.

Hundreds of artists have joined the movement in recent months with the likes of Massive Attack ,  Fontaines D.C. ,  Amyl & The Sniffers , and  Kneecap among the first leading names to join the initiative. They were soon joined by Paramore , Rina Sawayama , MIKE, Primal Scream , Faye Webster , Japanese Breakfast , Yaeji , King Krule , MJ Lenderman , Mannequin Pussy , Wednesday , Soccer Mommy and MØ .

Other major names to have thrown their weight behind ‘No Music For Genocide’ include Björk ,  Lorde, IDLES, MUNA, Paloma Faith ,  Clairo, Wolf Alice, Lucy Dacus and AURORA , My Bloody Valentine , Denzel Curry , Shygirl , Paris Paloma , Vacations, Innervisions and YHWH Nailgun .

items.title: ‘Nosferatu’ director Robert Eggers doesn’t want next film to be horror
items.summary:
Robert Eggers is “eager” for his next film to not be a horror after a string of dark, spooky projects.

READ MORE: ‘Nosferatu’ review: bloody, beautiful vampire remake is a bit of an empty vessel 

Eggers made his feature film debut in 2015 with gothic folk horror The Witch . He followed that up with 2019’s psychological horror The Lighthouse and 2022’s dark fantasy The Northman . In 2024, he wrote and directed gothic vampire horror Nosferatu and next month, his Werwulf hits cinemas.

“In 14th-century England, a mysterious creature stalks a foggy countryside as local folklore becomes a terrifying reality for the villagers,” reads the official synopsis, with another describing it as a tale of “devotion, damnation and the devil within.”

However, despite recent films about vampires and werewolves, Eggers has said he’s not looking to create an inter-connected universe of mythical beasts, and wants to do something outside of horror for his next project.

“I’m eager not to continue purposely doing Robert Eggers’ ‘House of Horror’,” he said during a Q+A recently. “I don’t need to do The Mummy or The Opera . Not to say that I won’t, but I think I need a break.”

Earlier this year, it was announced that Eggers would be working on a movie adaptation of William Shakespeare’s Romeo & Juliet . “After Werwulf, I was writing another horror movie, and it got so dark again. I was like, ‘I need a break. So, I’ll do something about two teenagers killing themselves’,” he said during a talk at Beyond Fest (via Deadline ).

It’s also been reported that Eggers is looking to remake Charles…
items.t: ‘Nosferatu’ director Robert Eggers doesn’t want next film to be horror

items.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ just broke the UK record for biggest documentary opening ever
items.summary:
You Can See Everything has broken the record for the biggest opening for a non-concert documentary in British history.

READ MORE: ‘You Can See Everything’ review: a three-hour odyssey of deception, doubt and dodgy dealings 

You Can See Everything was only unveiled in September at the 53rd Telluride Film Festival and hit US cinemas on October 16. The documentary follows filmmaker Nathan Fielder after he moves in with health businesswoman and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment in 2023.

The first trailer for You Can See Everything blew up across social media , with many comparing it to a living horror. When it launched in the US , the documentary took $5.5million (£4.2million) on its first day and across its opening weekend, took $15.6million (£11.9million) against a budget of $7million (£5.3million). It’s currently grossed more than $90million (68.7million) in the US.

You Can See Everything hit UK cinemas on Friday (November 20) and in its opening weekend, took $3.2million (£2.4million). That makes it the biggest opening for a non-concert documentary in the UK ever, beating the previous record of $1.7million (£1.3million) set by Michael Moore’s 2004 film Fahrenheit 9/11 (via Variety ).

With many screenings sold out, You Can See Everything is on-track to become the highest-grossing non-concert documentary in UK cinema history. The top three are currently March Of The Penguins ($4.3million, £3.2million), Amy ($5million, £3.8million) and Fahrenheit 9/11 ($8.5million, (£6.4million).

Speaking about the hype around the film,…
items.t: ‘You Can See Everything’ just broke the UK record for biggest documentary opening ever

items.title: ‘My name was poison’: Donny Osmond on fame, failure – and his friend Michael Jackson
items.summary:
He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse

For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US.

Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania.

Twelve months ago, when Interpol and Bloc Party announced a UK and European co-headline tour, the pairing looked like an even contest: two of 00s indie’s most revered acts, whose landmark debuts remain touchstones of the era.

items.title: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness
items.summary:
M&S Bank Arena, Liverpool
Just a few years since playing little dive bars, the Irish rockers have confidently scaled up to huge rooms like this – and are now one of the key interpreters of modern malaise

A mere seven years since their debut, Dogrel, Fontaines DC have enjoyed a virtually seamless passage from Dublin dive bars to arenas, with stadiums to follow next year. Each step has been taken seemingly effortlessly in their stride and this latest outing is no exception. Bathed in shimmering blue light, the band are well into hymnal opener Six Shot Morning before we even see sight of singer Grian Chatten. He wanders on while singing, an entrance worthy of Frank Sinatra.

Chatten has previously seemed to distrust showbiz, but if anything the singer seems far more comfortable on the bigger stage than he ever did on smaller ones. With his Korn T-shirt, unfeasibly baggy trousers and tiny tattoo reading “deadly” in capitals, he leaps around, raises his arms to whip up the crowd and points the microphone towards them to sing key lines. Similarly, music this intense, dark, elegiac and even bleak – which speaks to the void at the heart of much modern life – is hardly typical arena fare but works brilliantly by taking on a more anthemic, celebratory aspect. It’s certainly weirdly thrilling hearing Chatten’s lines such as “We’re all depressed, running on a wheel” or “I don’t feel anything in the modern world” – or a song as plainly dark as Jackie Down the Line – become enormous, arena-uniting sing-songs.
items.t: Fontaines DC review – thrilling gothic grandeur from a band vaulting into greatness

items.title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold
items.summary:
Isaac Eiger’s solo venture leaves jangle pop behind for a wilder sound. Often it owes a debt to Alex G, but what indie-rock song doesn’t these days?

From New York via Montana
Recommended if you like Cameron Winter, Tobias Jesso Jr, Alex G
Up next Supporting Caroline on tour in Canada and the US until 19 November

Isaac Eiger is something of a scene legend in the world of American indie-rock. Raised in Bozeman, Montana, he was the founder and lead singer of the cult shoegaze-adjacent six-piece Strange Ranger, who left heartbroken a small, fervent fanbase when they announced their breakup in 2023. Taking a discernibly British approach to their sound, Strange Ranger traversed C86-y jangle-pop before landing on Madchester rave-up for their final album, 2023’s Pure Music. But Eiger is nothing if not musically worldly: he has written and produced with both underground heroes (Cassandra Jenkins, Chanel Beads) and nascent pop stars (Adéla, Frost Children).

Ever-prolific, Eiger also has a solo project under the name Threshold, with which he released a gauzy, 19-minute EP in 2024 called Thief. Earlier this year, he released Stillwater, the first single from the debut Threshold album, due for release in 2027 on the London-based label Untitled. items.title: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming
items.summary:
(CDR)
Based around sounds recorded on her trips back to China, the Fujian-born, London-based producer creates a curious nocturnal collage on Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming

Lucid dreaming is one of the influences behind Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, the new record from Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z. “Every night is an adventure,” she writes in the liner notes, “I can even smell things in certain dreams.” The eight tracks here are suitably sensory, scattered with effervescent sounds, ephemeral whispers and polyrhythmic percussion.

Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which the echoes of words gradually reveal themselves among the fizzing, softly discordant arrangement: a warped, increasingly urgent call to “wake up”, reminiscent of the foggy state as you rise from sleep. Z amplifies this heady feeling later on in Exit, Elsewhere, where her overlapping narration and rattling bells cause total disorientation.

items.title: Take That: Dreamers review – 50-something boyband fail to relight the fire on nostalgia-drenched return
items.summary:
(EMI)
The pallid disco revivalism sounds like S Club 7 and the folksy stomp-clap like Mumford and Sons – yet a few standout moments prove they can still strike gold if they try

Listening to Wonderkids, the string-laden opener of Take That’s new album, it seems the three remaining fiftysomething boybanders are feeling reflective. “Forgiving you, forgiving me / This vicious circle is now complete,” sings Gary Barlow.

In the years since their last record, the band – and former member Robbie Williams – have indeed laid out the trials and tribulations of 35 years of Take That in several documentaries, some more candid than others. Earlier this year, they even embarked on a revival of their blockbuster 2009 Circus tour. Unfortunately, all this reminiscing has left their 10th album feeling so steeped in nostalgia that any moments of greatness struggle for attention.

items.title: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel
items.summary:
From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas

Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”

It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in…

items.title: Is Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages the year’s wildest electronic album?
items.summary:
(Warp)
The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres

The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”.

A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. Accordingly, his albums to date have dealt in what approving critics like to call deconstructions or interrogations of dance music rather than dance music itself: 2012’s Quantum Jelly and 2014’s Superimpositions featured what Senni called “pointillistic trance”, spinning the icy, staccato notes and arpeggiated synth lines of the genre’s epic breakdowns into lengthy, beatless tracks that never reached the climax implied.
